# Cutaneous warts

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Cutaneous warts*

[Original Article Link](/library/sE0tC3)

---

## Summary

Cutaneous warts are common benign cutaneous lesions caused by the <u>skin</u>-to-<u>skin</u> transmission of <u>human papillomavirus</u> (<u>HPV</u>). Types include <u>common warts</u>, <u>flat warts</u>, <u>plantar warts</u>, and <u>filiform warts</u>. Cutaneous warts appear as solitary or multiple <u>skin</u>-colored <u>hyperkeratotic</u> <u>exophytic</u> <u>papules</u> or <u>plaques</u>. Lesions are typically asymptomatic but sometimes cause <u>pain</u> or discomfort. Diagnosis is clinical; pinpoint dots on the surface of the lesions that bleed on shaving are a characteristic feature. <u>Biopsy</u> may be considered if there is diagnostic uncertainty. Most cutaneous warts resolve spontaneously within two years, but recurrence is common. Initial management options include <u>watchful waiting</u>, <u>topical salicylic acid</u>, or <u>cryotherapy</u>. Options for refractory warts include electrocauterization, <u>photodynamic therapy</u>, topical immunotherapy, and <u>intralesional injections</u>.




See also “<u>HPV infection</u>” and “<u>Anogenital warts</u>.”

---

## Etiology

* <u>HPV types that infect the cutaneous epithelium</u>, e.g.: [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)

* <u>Common warts</u> and <u>plantar warts</u>: <u>HPV</u> types 1–4, 27, and 29

* <u>Flat warts</u>: <u>HPV</u> types 3, 10, 28, and 29

* Transmission: direct <u>skin</u> contact (including <u>autoinoculation</u>) or <u>fomites</u> [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)

---

## Clinical features

Warts manifest as discrete or grouped lesions, and the distribution is often more extensive in individuals with underlying <u>immunodeficiency</u>. [[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)




### Common warts (<u>verrucae vulgaris</u>) [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)




* <u>Skin</u>-colored or gray-brown <u>exophytic</u> <u>papules</u> or <u>plaques</u> (<u>verrucous</u> lesions)

* <u>Hyperkeratotic</u>, rough surface

* May contain red, brown, or black dots

* Located on the hands, knees, and/or face

* Usually painless [[4]](/library/Bedza60)





![Common warts](media/x8db1wn321ebdfvmt0re95zf.jpg)

Common warts

![Common warts (verrucae vulgares)](media/odfzdencmspbumv3ag9k04is.jpg)

Common warts (verrucae vulgares)




### Flat warts (<u>verrucae planae</u>) [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)




* More common in children than adults

* Yellow-brown <u>papules</u> with a smooth, flat surface

* Typically occur on face, back of the hands, and shins  [[5]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Scratching can cause a linear distribution. [[5]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Usually painless. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)





![Flat warts (verrucae planae)](media/s3e3r7ysoo054qbcgskoc1s1.jpg)

Flat warts (verrucae planae)




### Plantar warts (<u>verrucae plantares</u>)  [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)




* <u>Hyperkeratotic</u> <u>papules</u> or <u>plaques</u> on the soles of the feet  [[5]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Small black dots may be visible on the surface.

* Multiple warts may become confluent (a mosaic wart). [[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)

* Can be painful





![Plantar wart](media/u4vuz9qd2c1vh9tla4rn337b.jpg)

Plantar wart

![Plantar wart](media/z5g0z59km8507mif87o1lj4k.jpg)

Plantar wart




### Filiform warts [[4]](/library/Bedza60)




* Single or multiple finger-like projections from a narrow base [[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)[[5]](/library/Wk1P5S0)

* Most commonly seen on the face and/or neck





![Filiform wart](media/j2grlyg3dl35ji31mdvizmn5.jpg)

Filiform wart

---

## Diagnosis

* Diagnosis is typically clinical. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>Dermoscopy</u> can show red, brown, or black dots.  [[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)

* Shaving the surface of the wart causes bleeding.  [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[6]](/library/FC0gFR)

* Consider <u>biopsy</u> if there is diagnostic uncertainty.  [[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Callus</u>

* <u>Corn</u>

* <u>Molluscum contagiosum</u>

* <u>Syringoma</u>

* <u>Seborrheic keratosis</u>

* <u>Actinic keratosis</u>

* <u>Keratoacanthoma</u>

* <u>Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### General principles




* Consider <u>watchful waiting</u>, as most warts resolve within two years. [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)

* Indications for treatment include: [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)

* Discomfort

* Patient preference and cosmesis

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>

* Refractory warts

* Educate patients on <u>prevention of cutaneous warts</u> to reduce <u>autoinoculation</u>.





### First-line options [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[7]](/library/R4dlQJ0)




* <u>Topical salicylic acid</u> DOSAGE (avoid on the face)  [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[3]](/library/lPWvUl0)

* <u>Cryotherapy</u>

* Can be painful

* Requires multiple sessions (repeated every 2–4 weeks, max. 6 sessions) [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[6]](/library/FC0gFR)

* Consider <u>topical salicylic acid</u> between sessions. [[6]](/library/FC0gFR)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>topical salicylic acid</u> on the face because of the risk of pigmentation changes. [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)




### Options for refractory warts [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[6]](/library/FC0gFR)




Refer patients with refractory warts to dermatology. The following treatments may be considered, although there is limited evidence to support their <u>efficacy</u>.




* <u>Photodynamic therapy</u>

* Topical immunotherapy  or antiproliferative agents

* <u>Intralesional injection</u> of <u>bleomycin</u>, bivalent or quadrivalent <u>HPV vaccine</u>, or <u>Candida</u> or <u>mumps</u> <u>skin</u> <u>antigen</u> [[1]](/library/RPWlel0)[[8]](/library/OidI7p0)

* Laser therapy

* Electrocauterization or <u>curettage</u>





> [!TIP]
> Recurrence is common. Combination therapy or multiple treatments are often required. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)




> [!WARNING]
> To prevent aerosolized transmission of <u>HPV</u> to the <u>upper respiratory tract</u>, electrocauterization of warts should be performed in an adequately ventilated area with appropriate <u>PPE</u> (e.g., N95 or above grade <u>respirator</u>). [[9]](/library/KQdUCp0)
